claim: ZNRF3 is a transmembrane E3 ubiquitin ligase that targets Wnt receptors for ubiquitination and lysosomal degradation.
source: Zinc and ring finger 3 (ZNRF3) is a transmembrane E3 ubiquitin ligase that targets Wnt receptors for ubiquitination and lysosomal degradation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations to previous work (Hao et al., 2012; Koo et al., 2012) in the introduction.

claim: Dephosphorylation of an endocytic tyrosine motif (4Y motif) in ZNRF3 by PTPRK promotes ZNRF3 internalization and Wnt receptor degradation.
source: Previously, we showed that dephosphorylation of an endocytic tyrosine motif (4Y motif) in ZNRF3 by protein tyrosine phosphatase receptor-type kappa (PTPRK) promotes ZNRF3 internalization and Wnt receptor degradation (Chang et al 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors (Chang et al 2020).

claim: MET is a 4Y kinase that phosphorylates the endocytic tyrosine motif in ZNRF3.
source: Here we identify the proto-oncogene MET (mesenchymal-epithelial transition factor) as a 4Y kinase.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the manuscript supported by multiple experimental data including kinase screening, overexpression, and knockdown experiments shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: MET binds to ZNRF3.
source: Here we identify the proto-oncogene MET (mesenchymal-epithelial transition factor) as a 4Y kinase. MET binds to ZNRF3 and induces 4Y phosphorylation, stimulated by the MET ligand HGF (hepatocyte growth factor, scatter factor).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 3C.

claim: MET induces 4Y phosphorylation of ZNRF3.
source: MET binds to ZNRF3 and induces 4Y phosphorylation, stimulated by the MET ligand HGF (hepatocyte growth factor, scatter factor).
evidence: This is supported by phospho-tyrosine immunoblot data shown in Figures 1D, 2A-B, and 3A-D.

claim: HGF stimulates MET-mediated 4Y phosphorylation of ZNRF3.
source: MET binds to ZNRF3 and induces 4Y phosphorylation, stimulated by the MET ligand HGF (hepatocyte growth factor, scatter factor).
evidence: This is supported by data showing HGF treatment increases pTyr-ZNRF3 (Figure 3A-D).

claim: HGF-MET signaling reduces ZNRF3-dependent Wnt receptor degradation.
source: HGF-MET signaling reduces ZNRF3-dependent Wnt receptor degradation thereby enhancing Wnt/β-catenin signaling.
evidence: This is supported by data showing HGF protects FZD5 and LRP6 from ZNRF3-mediated degradation (Figure 5A-C).

claim: HGF-MET signaling enhances Wnt/β-catenin signaling.
source: HGF-MET signaling reduces ZNRF3-dependent Wnt receptor degradation thereby enhancing Wnt/β-catenin signaling.
evidence: This is supported by data showing HGF treatment increases β-catenin accumulation upon Wnt3a stimulation (Figure 5D-E).

claim: Depletion of MET promotes the internalization of ZNRF3.
source: Conversely, depletion or pharmacological inhibition of MET promotes the internalization of ZNRF3 and Wnt receptor degradation.
evidence: This is supported by cell surface biotinylation data showing reduced surface ZNRF3 upon MET knockdown (Figure 4B).

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of MET promotes the internalization of ZNRF3.
source: Conversely, depletion or pharmacological inhibition of MET promotes the internalization of ZNRF3 and Wnt receptor degradation.
evidence: This is supported by cell surface biotinylation data showing reduced surface ZNRF3 upon Crizotinib treatment (Figure 4A).

claim: Depletion of MET promotes Wnt receptor degradation.
source: Conversely, depletion or pharmacological inhibition of MET promotes the internalization of ZNRF3 and Wnt receptor degradation.
evidence: This is supported by data showing reduced LRP6 levels upon MET inhibition (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of MET promotes Wnt receptor degradation.
source: Conversely, depletion or pharmacological inhibition of MET promotes the internalization of ZNRF3 and Wnt receptor degradation.
evidence: This is supported by data showing reduced LRP6 levels upon Crizotinib treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).

claim: HGF-MET signaling phosphorylates ZNRF3 and PTPRK dephosphorylates ZNRF3 to regulate ZNRF3 internalization, functioning as a rheostat for Wnt signaling.
source: We conclude that HGF-MET signaling phosphorylates- and PTPRK dephosphorylates ZNRF3 to regulate ZNRF3 internalization, functioning as a rheostat for Wnt signaling that may offer novel opportunities for therapeutic intervention.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the manuscript, supported by data showing opposing effects of MET and PTPRK on ZNRF3 phosphorylation (Figure 2F) and the effects on Wnt signaling.

claim: The MET-PTPRK rheostat for Wnt signaling may offer novel opportunities for therapeutic intervention.
source: We conclude that HGF-MET signaling phosphorylates- and PTPRK dephosphorylates ZNRF3 to regulate ZNRF3 internalization, functioning as a rheostat for Wnt signaling that may offer novel opportunities for therapeutic intervention.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential therapeutic applications based on the findings.

claim: Wnt signaling plays a pivotal role in embryonic development and in maintaining organ homeostasis.
source: Wnt signaling plays a pivotal role in embryonic development and in maintaining organ homeostasis (MacDonald et al., 2009; Clevers and Nusse, 2012; Kim et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Wnt signaling is tightly regulated at numerous levels of the pathway.
source: Wnt signaling is tightly regulated at numerous levels of the pathway (Niehrs, 2012; Nusse and Clevers, 2017; Anthony et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Wnt receptor availability at the plasma membrane is controlled by ER chaperones.
source: In addition, Wnt receptor availability at the plasma membrane is controlled by ER chaperones (Hsieh et al., 2003; Weekes et al., 2012; Berger et al., 2017) as well as by the E3 ubiquitin ligase ZNRF3 and its functional homolog RNF43.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Wnt receptor availability at the plasma membrane is controlled by the E3 ubiquitin ligase ZNRF3 and its functional homolog RNF43.
source: In addition, Wnt receptor availability at the plasma membrane is controlled by ER chaperones (Hsieh et al., 2003; Weekes et al., 2012; Berger et al., 2017) as well as by the E3 ubiquitin ligase ZNRF3 and its functional homolog RNF43.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Hao et al., 2012; Koo et al., 2012).

claim: ZNRF3 and RNF43 act as negative feedback regulators of Wnt signaling that promote receptor degradation by ubiquitylating and internalizing cell surface LRP6 and FZD.
source: These transmembrane proteins act as negative feedback regulators of Wnt signaling that promote receptor degradation by ubiquitylating and internalizing cell surface LRP6 and FZD (Hao et al., 2012; Koo et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: ZNRF3 internalizes and degrades the BMP receptor type 1A and thereby antagonizes BMP signaling.
source: More recently, ZNRF3 was shown to also internalize and degrade the BMP receptor type 1A and thereby antagonize BMP signaling (Lee et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent work.

claim: ZNRF3/RNF43 are counteracted by secreted proteins of the R-spondin family, which sequester ZNRF3/RNF43 in conjunction with LGR4/5/6, thereby leading to the membrane clearance of ZNRF3/RNF43.
source: ZNRF3/RNF43 are counteracted by secreted proteins of the R-spondin family, which sequester ZNRF3/RNF43 in conjunction with LGR4/5/6, thereby leading to the membrane clearance of ZNRF3/RNF43 (Carmon et al., 2011; de Lau et al., 2011; Glinka et al., 2011; Hao et al., 2012; Koo et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: ZNRF3 and RNF43 play important roles in adult stem cells and in tumorigenesis.
source: ZNRF3 and RNF43 play important roles in adult stem cells and in tumorigenesis (de Lau et al., 2014; Hao et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Little is known about how ZNRF3 and RNF43 are regulated intracellularly.
source: Yet, little is known about how ZNRF3 and RNF43 are regulated intracellularly (Jiang et al., 2015; Ci et al., 2018; Giebel et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field, supported by limited citations.

claim: The cytoplasmic domain of ZNRF3 contains an endocytic signal consisting of four consecutive tyrosine residues (4Y motif: YETMYQHYY) that regulates ZNRF3- and in turn Wnt receptor internalization.
source: We recently discovered an endocytic signal in the cytoplasmic domain of ZNRF3 consisting of four consecutive tyrosine residues (4Y motif: YETMYQHYY) that regulates ZNRF3- and in turn Wnt receptor internalization (Chang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Tyrosine motifs play a critical role in regulating endocytosis of transmembrane proteins.
source: Tyrosine motifs play a critical role in regulating endocytosis of transmembrane proteins and unphosphorylated YXXXφ and φXXY sites as well as YXXφ (φ = bulky hydrophobic amino acid) serve as internalization motifs (Zhang and Allison, 1997; Roush et al., 1998; Bonifacino and Traub, 2003; Royle et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Unphosphorylated YXXXφ and φXXY sites as well as YXXφ serve as internalization motifs.
source: Tyrosine motifs play a critical role in regulating endocytosis of transmembrane proteins and unphosphorylated YXXXφ and φXXY sites as well as YXXφ (φ = bulky hydrophobic amino acid) serve as internalization motifs (Zhang and Allison, 1997; Roush et al., 1998; Bonifacino and Traub, 2003; Royle et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Phosphorylation of the 4Y motif prevents ZNRF3 internalization and stabilizes Wnt receptors at the cell surface.
source: Phosphorylation of the 4Y motif prevents ZNRF3 internalization and stabilizes Wnt receptors at the cell surface.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Chang et al., 2020) and data in the current manuscript.

claim: Dephosphorylation of the 4Y motif by PTPRK promotes ZNRF3 internalization and Wnt receptor clearance from the cell surface, thereby inhibiting Wnt signaling.
source: Conversely, dephosphorylation of the 4Y motif by PTPRK (protein tyrosine phosphatase receptor-type kappa) promotes ZNRF3 internalization and Wnt receptor clearance from the cell surface, thereby inhibiting Wnt signaling (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Chang et al., 2020) and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Eighteen tyrosine kinases were selected by combined in silico prediction and reported cellular localization for screening as candidate 4Y kinases.
source: Eighteen tyrosine kinases were selected by combined in silico prediction and reported cellular localization.
evidence: This is described in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Inhibition of SRC family kinases (SFKs), focal adhesion kinase (FAK), and MET showed significant reduction on pTyr-ZNRF3 in the kinase inhibitor screen.
source: Among 18 selected candidate kinases, inhibition of SRC family kinases (SFKs), focal adhesion kinase (FAK; encoded by PTK2), and MET showed significant reduction on pTyr-ZNRF3 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the kinase inhibitor screening data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Overexpression of MET strongly phosphorylates ZNRF3.
source: Overexpression of MET strongly- and SRC weakly phosphorylated ZNRF3 (lanes 5–6), while FAK (lane 7) had no effect.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Overexpression of SRC weakly phosphorylates ZNRF3.
source: Overexpression of MET strongly- and SRC weakly phosphorylated ZNRF3 (lanes 5–6), while FAK (lane 7) had no effect.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Overexpression of FAK has no effect on ZNRF3 phosphorylation.
source: Overexpression of MET strongly- and SRC weakly phosphorylated ZNRF3 (lanes 5–6), while FAK (lane 7) had no effect.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: SRC, YES, and FYN are widely expressed SFKs with overlapping functions.
source: SRC, YES, and FYN are widely expressed SFKs with overlapping functions (Stein et al., 1994; Thomas et al., 1995), but we counted-out YES as candidate since a YES-specific inhibitor had no effect in the initial screen.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: YES was excluded as a candidate 4Y kinase because a YES-specific inhibitor had no effect in the initial screen.
source: SRC, YES, and FYN are widely expressed SFKs with overlapping functions (Stein et al., 1994; Thomas et al., 1995), but we counted-out YES as candidate since a YES-specific inhibitor had no effect in the initial screen.
evidence: This is based on data from the kinase inhibitor screen.

claim: Depletion of MET reduces ZNRF3 phosphorylation.
source: We therefore continued with individual or combined knockdown of SRC, FYN, and MET by siRNAs and found that depletion of all three kinases, most prominently of MET, reduced ZNRF3 phosphorylation (Figure 2A; compare lane 2 to lanes 3, 4, or 6).
evidence: This is supported by siRNA knockdown data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Triple knockdown of SRC, FYN, and MET nearly eliminates pTyr-ZNRF3 signal to background.
source: Triple knockdown of SRC, FYN, and MET nearly eliminated the pTyr signal to background (lanes 7 vs. 1).
evidence: This is supported by siRNA knockdown data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: H1703 cells harbor normal MET copy number.
source: Of note, while MET is often amplified in cancer cells, H1703 cells harbor normal MET copy number (Kubo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The activity of SFKs as monitored by pY416 autophosphorylation is unchanged upon knockdown of MET.
source: However, the activity of SFKs as monitored by pY416 autophosphorylation was unchanged upon knockdown of MET (Figure 2A), suggesting that MET directly regulates pTyr-ZNRF3 independently of SFKs.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: MET directly regulates pTyr-ZNRF3 independently of SFKs.
source: However, the activity of SFKs as monitored by pY416 autophosphorylation was unchanged upon knockdown of MET (Figure 2A), suggesting that MET directly regulates pTyr-ZNRF3 independently of SFKs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that MET knockdown reduces ZNRF3 phosphorylation without affecting SFK activity.

claim: ZNRF3 robustly binds to endogenous MET.
source: Moreover, ZNRF3 robustly bound to endogenous MET, whereas no binding to SRC was detected (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: ZNRF3 does not bind to SRC.
source: Moreover, ZNRF3 robustly bound to endogenous MET, whereas no binding to SRC was detected (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: ZNRF3 phosphorylation by MET is dramatically reduced with ZNRF3(∆4Y), although not completely abolished, suggesting some 4Y-independent phosphorylation by MET.
source: ZNRF3 phosphorylation by MET was dramatically reduced with ZNRF3(∆4Y), although not completely abolished, suggesting some 4Y-independent phosphorylation by MET.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2E and represents an inference from the data.

claim: SRC-mediated ZNRF3 phosphorylation shows a strong increase with ZNRF3(∆4Y) compared to wild-type ZNRF3.
source: In contrast, no reduction but a strong increase was observed for SRC-mediated ZNRF3 phosphorylation (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: ZNRF3(∆4Y) preferentially localizes at the cell surface.
source: This unexpected increase may be explained by our previous observation that ZNRF3(∆4Y) preferentially localizes at the cell surface (Chang et al., 2020) where activated SRC also resides.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Activated SRC resides at the cell surface.
source: This unexpected increase may be explained by our previous observation that ZNRF3(∆4Y) preferentially localizes at the cell surface (Chang et al., 2020) where activated SRC also resides.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge to explain the observation.

claim: Enhanced pTyr-ZNRF3 induced by PTPRK siRNA depletion is rescued by Crizotinib.
source: Indeed, enhanced pTyr-ZNRF3 induced by PTPRK siRNA depletion was rescued by Crizotinib (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: MET and PTPRK oppose each other in ZNRF3 4Y phosphorylation.
source: This PTPRK-MET double-inhibition experiment supports that MET and PTPRK oppose each other in ZNRF3 4Y phosphorylation (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is an inference based on the rescue experiment shown in Figure 2F.

claim: MET is both necessary and sufficient for 4Y phosphorylation.
source: Taken together, our results show that MET binds ZNRF3 and is both necessary and sufficient for 4Y phosphorylation, supporting the notion that MET is indeed a 4Y kinase that opposes PTPRK.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple experiments including overexpression, knockdown, and inhibitor studies.

claim: MET is likely not the only 4Y kinase since in early Xenopus embryos, ZNRF3 dephosphorylation by PTPRK plays a role during Spemann organizer patterning before the onset of significant Met expression.
source: Of note, MET is likely not the only 4Y kinase since in early Xenopus embryos, ZNRF3 dephosphorylation by PTPRK plays a role during Spemann organizer patterning (Chang et al., 2020) before the onset of significant Met expression (Koibuchi et al., 2004) and hence we did not analyze Met in Xenopus.
evidence: This is an inference based on developmental timing data from Xenopus, supported by citations.

claim: SRC promotes ZNRF3 phosphorylation likely at a site different from the 4Y motif.
source: SRC on the other hand promotes ZNRF3 phosphorylation likely at a site different from the 4Y motif and was not further analyzed.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that SRC phosphorylates ZNRF3 but phosphorylation increases with the 4Y deletion mutant.

claim: HGF strongly induces pTyr-ZNRF3.
source: Indeed, HGF strongly induced pTyr-ZNRF3, and this induction was reduced by the MET inhibitor Crizotinib (Figure 3A), as well as by siRNA-mediated knockdown of MET (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: HGF-induced pTyr-ZNRF3 is reduced by the MET inhibitor Crizotinib.
source: Indeed, HGF strongly induced pTyr-ZNRF3, and this induction was reduced by the MET inhibitor Crizotinib (Figure 3A), as well as by siRNA-mediated knockdown of MET (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: HGF-induced pTyr-ZNRF3 is reduced by siRNA-mediated knockdown of MET.
source: Indeed, HGF strongly induced pTyr-ZNRF3, and this induction was reduced by the MET inhibitor Crizotinib (Figure 3A), as well as by siRNA-mediated knockdown of MET (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: HGF treatment increases the binding of ZNRF3 to endogenous MET in a time-dependent fashion, peaking at 30 min of HGF treatment.
source: Moreover, Co-IP analysis showed that HGF treatment increased the binding of ZNRF3 to endogenous MET in a time-dependent fashion, peaking at 30 min of HGF treatment (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Total MET levels slightly decrease after 15 min HGF treatment, likely reflecting ligand-induced MET internalization and degradation.
source: Increased binding of ZNRF3 to MET occurred despite total MET levels slightly decreasing after 15 min HGF treatment, the latter likely reflecting ligand-induced MET internalization and degradation (Taher et al., 2002).
evidence: This is an observation from Figure 3C with an inference about the mechanism supported by citation.

claim: HGF strongly induces phosphorylation of wild-type ZNRF3 but barely affects phosphorylation of ZNRF3(∆4Y).
source: Furthermore, while HGF strongly induced phosphorylation of Wt ZNRF3, phosphorylation of ZNRF3(∆4Y) was barely affected (Figure 3D), corroborating that HGF-MET signaling mainly targets the 4Y motif.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: HGF-MET signaling mainly targets the 4Y motif.
source: Furthermore, while HGF strongly induced phosphorylation of Wt ZNRF3, phosphorylation of ZNRF3(∆4Y) was barely affected (Figure 3D), corroborating that HGF-MET signaling mainly targets the 4Y motif.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effect of HGF on wild-type vs. 4Y deletion mutant ZNRF3.

claim: Crizotinib reduces cell surface levels of ZNRF3.
source: To test these predictions we performed cell surface biotinylation assays and monitored ZNRF3. To antagonize MET signaling, we employed Crizotinib and MET siRNA, both of which reduced cell surface levels of ZNRF3 (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This is supported by cell surface biotinylation data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: MET siRNA reduces cell surface levels of ZNRF3.
source: To test these predictions we performed cell surface biotinylation assays and monitored ZNRF3. To antagonize MET signaling, we employed Crizotinib and MET siRNA, both of which reduced cell surface levels of ZNRF3 (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This is supported by cell surface biotinylation data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Neither the FAK inhibitor TAE226 nor the SFK inhibitor Dasatinib changes cell surface ZNRF3 levels.
source: In contrast, neither the FAK inhibitor TAE226 nor the SFK inhibitor Dasatinib changed cell surface ZNRF3 levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is supported by cell surface biotinylation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: HGF treatment increases ZNRF3 surface levels in a time-dependent manner, plateauing after ~45 min.
source: Conversely, HGF treatment increased ZNRF3 surface levels in a time-dependent manner, plateauing after ~45 min (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by cell surface biotinylation data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: HGF-MET signaling stabilizes ZNRF3 at the cell surface consistent with a role in phosphorylating and masking the endocytic 4Y motif.
source: We conclude that HGF-MET signaling stabilizes ZNRF3 at the cell surface consistent with a role in phosphorylating and masking the endocytic 4Y motif (Figure 4D–E).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the cell surface biotinylation data and the model illustrated in Figure 4D-E.

claim: Overexpression of ZNRF3 reduces mature FZD5 levels.
source: Overexpression of ZNRF3 reduced mature FZD5 levels as previously reported (Hao et al., 2012; Koo et al., 2012; Giebel et al., 2021) (compare lanes 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5A and citations to previous work.

claim: HGF reverses ZNRF3-mediated reduction of FZD5 after 90 min treatment.
source: Overexpression of ZNRF3 reduced mature FZD5 levels as previously reported (Hao et al., 2012; Koo et al., 2012; Giebel et al., 2021) (compare lanes 1 and 2). HGF reversed this reduction after 90 min treatment (lanes 7–8).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: HGF treatment rescues reduced FZD5 levels in wild-type ZNRF3- but hardly in ZNRF3(∆4Y) transfected cells.
source: Strikingly, HGF treatment rescued reduced FZD5 levels in Wt ZNRF3- but hardly in ZNRF3(∆4Y) transfected cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: HGF specifically increases mature LRP6 levels within 1 hr treatment.
source: HGF specifically increased mature LRP6 levels within 1 hr treatment, and this increase by HGF was drastically abolished by siZNRF3/RNF43 treatment, which constitutively increased LRP6 levels (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The increase in LRP6 by HGF is drastically abolished by siZNRF3/RNF43 treatment.
source: HGF specifically increased mature LRP6 levels within 1 hr treatment, and this increase by HGF was drastically abolished by siZNRF3/RNF43 treatment, which constitutively increased LRP6 levels (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: siZNRF3/RNF43 treatment constitutively increases LRP6 levels.
source: HGF specifically increased mature LRP6 levels within 1 hr treatment, and this increase by HGF was drastically abolished by siZNRF3/RNF43 treatment, which constitutively increased LRP6 levels (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Inhibiting MET with Crizotinib reduces mature LRP6 in H3122 cells, an effect that is almost abolished when ZNRF3/RNF43 are siRNA-inhibited.
source: We tested an alternative lung adenocarcinoma cell line, H3122, and inhibiting MET with Crizotinib reduced mature LRP6, an effect that was almost abolished when ZNRF3/RNF43 where siRNA-inhibited (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: MET signaling is necessary and sufficient for LRP6 regulation via ZNRF3 in multiple lung cancer cell lines.
source: Taken together the results support that MET signaling is necessary and sufficient for LRP6 regulation via ZNRF3 and in multiple lung cancer cell lines.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on data from H1703 and H3122 cell lines.

claim: ZNRF3 and RNF43 can heterodimerize.
source: Of note, despite the fact that it does not contain any obvious endocytic Tyr motifs, we also knocked down RNF43 in the above experiments, because ZNRF3 and RNF43 can heterodimerize (Yu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Combined HGF and Wnt3a treatment synergizes to induce β-catenin accumulation.
source: Consistently, combined HGF and Wnt3a treatment synergized to induce β-catenin accumulation (Figure 5D–E).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5D-E.

claim: The HGF effect on β-catenin accumulation is MET-dependent.
source: Moreover, the HGF effect was MET- and ZNRF3/RNF43 dependent (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, C), confirming that HGF-MET promotes Wnt signaling via ZNRF3/RNF43.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The HGF effect on β-catenin accumulation is ZNRF3/RNF43 dependent.
source: Moreover, the HGF effect was MET- and ZNRF3/RNF43 dependent (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, C), confirming that HGF-MET promotes Wnt signaling via ZNRF3/RNF43.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: HGF-MET promotes Wnt signaling via ZNRF3/RNF43.
source: Moreover, the HGF effect was MET- and ZNRF3/RNF43 dependent (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, C), confirming that HGF-MET promotes Wnt signaling via ZNRF3/RNF43.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the dependency experiments.

claim: HGF and RSPO3 strongly synergize in inducing β-catenin accumulation.
source: Interestingly, HGF and RSPO3 strongly synergized in inducing β-catenin accumulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that they act non-redundantly.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: HGF and RSPO3 act non-redundantly.
source: Interestingly, HGF and RSPO3 strongly synergized in inducing β-catenin accumulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that they act non-redundantly.
evidence: This is an inference based on the synergistic effect observed.

claim: The ZNRF3 4Y motif is a phospho-regulated molecular rheostat of endocytosis.
source: Taken together, these results support a model whereby the ZNRF3 4Y motif is a phospho-regulated molecular rheostat of endocytosis: HGF-MET signaling impairs ZNRF3 function via phosphorylating and masking its endocytic 4Y motif, leading to accumulation of Wnt receptors and enhanced Wnt signalling, which is opposed by PTPRK (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is the main model of the manuscript, supported by all the data presented and illustrated in Figure 5F.

claim: The phosphorylated 4Y motif conforms to a MET consensus phosphorylation site.
source: Several lines of evidence support that MET directly phosphorylates ZNRF3: the phosphorylated 4Y motif conforms to a MET consensus phosphorylation site, MET is both necessary and sufficient for ZNRF3 phosphorylation, HGF stimulates ZNRF3 phosphorylation, and MET binds and phosphorylates ZNRF3 in a HGF-dependent manner.
evidence: This is stated as one line of evidence supporting direct phosphorylation, likely based on sequence analysis.

claim: MET dimerization or autophosphorylation is important for MET-ZNRF3 interaction.
source: The fact that HGF stimulates ZNRF3 binding suggests that MET dimerization or autophosphorylation is important for their interaction.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that HGF stimulates binding.

claim: MET complexes with a remarkably diverse set of other transmembrane proteins, notably cell adhesion molecules and other RTKs, thereby acting as a hub for signal integration and amplification.
source: Indeed, MET is known to complex with a remarkably diverse set of other transmembrane proteins, notably cell adhesion molecules and other RTKs, thereby acting as a hub for signal integration and amplification (Crepaldi et al., 1997; Follenzi et al., 2000; Jo et al., 2000; Trusolino et al., 2001; Giordano et al., 2002; Orian-Rousseau et al., 2002; Tanizaki et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Additional 4Y kinases besides MET may exist.
source: It is likely that MET is not the only 4Y kinase since in early Xenopus embryos, ZNRF3 dephosphorylation by PTPRK plays a role in Spemann organizer patterning at a stage that precedes significant zygotic expression of Xenopus Met (Koibuchi et al., 2004). Additional 4Y kinases besides MET may also explain while we failed to observe a role for MET in HEK29T cells (data not shown).
evidence: This is an inference based on developmental timing in Xenopus and cell-type specific observations.

claim: Autophosphorylation of the MET kinase domain at Tyr1234/1235 is critical for kinase activation.
source: Autophosphorylation of the MET kinase domain at Tyr1234/1235 is critical for kinase activation and in vitro, a Tyr1235 phosphopeptide is dephosphorylated by several PTPRK-like phosphatases (Barr et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: A Tyr1235 phosphopeptide of MET is dephosphorylated by several PTPRK-like phosphatases in vitro.
source: Autophosphorylation of the MET kinase domain at Tyr1234/1235 is critical for kinase activation and in vitro, a Tyr1235 phosphopeptide is dephosphorylated by several PTPRK-like phosphatases (Barr et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In HEK293 cells PTPRJ/DEP-1 dephosphorylates MET phospho-sites required for adapter protein binding.
source: Moreover, in HEK293 cells PTPRJ/DEP-1 dephosphorylates MET phospho-sites required for adapter protein binding (Palka et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: MET kinase and PTPRK phosphatase may cross-regulate each other in a ternary complex with ZNRF3.
source: Since both MET and PTPRK bind ZNRF3, it will be interesting to explore if all three proteins form a ternary complex in which MET kinase-PTPRK phosphatase cross regulate each other.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research directions.

claim: R-spondins bind ZNRF3 in conjunction with LGR4 and co-internalize the complex to remove ZNRF3, thereby de-repressing Wnt receptors.
source: However, they do so in an opposite manner: R-spondins bind ZNRF3 in conjunction with LGR4 and co-internalize the complex to remove ZNRF3, thereby de-repressing Wnt receptors (Carmon et al., 2011; de Lau et al., 2011; Glinka et al., 2011; Hao et al., 2012; Koo et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: HGF prevents ZNRF3 co-internalization of Wnt receptors by inducing ZNRF3-MET association and 4Y phosphorylation.
source: HGF does the opposite: it prevents ZNRF3 co-internalization of Wnt receptors by inducing ZNRF3-MET association and 4Y phosphorylation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: HGF-MET and R-spondins may target either distinct ZNRF3 surface complexes or different endocytic routes.
source: This apparent paradox may be due to HGF-MET and R-spondins targeting either distinct ZNRF3 surface complexes or different endocytic routes.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for how both promoting and impairing endocytosis can inhibit ZNRF3.

claim: R-spondins might co-internalize and reduce MET levels at the cell surface.
source: Relatedly, since MET binds ZNRF3, it will be interesting to test if R-spondins might co-internalize and reduce MET levels at the cell surface.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research directions.

claim: HGF and RSPO3 strongly synergize in inducing β-catenin accumulation, supporting that they target distinct ZNRF3 pools.
source: The observation that HGF and RSPO3 strongly synergize in inducing β-catenin accumulation supports that they target distinct ZNRF3 pools and raises the possibility that HGF may be useful in growing Wnt-dependent organoids.
evidence: This is an inference based on the synergy data.

claim: HGF may be useful in growing Wnt-dependent organoids.
source: The observation that HGF and RSPO3 strongly synergize in inducing β-catenin accumulation supports that they target distinct ZNRF3 pools and raises the possibility that HGF may be useful in growing Wnt-dependent organoids.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications.

claim: The net effect of HGF-MET signaling is to stabilize Wnt receptors and β-catenin.
source: We show that the net effect of HGF-MET signaling is to stabilize Wnt receptors and β-catenin.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data showing effects on FZD5, LRP6, and β-catenin.

claim: HGF-MET signaling in renal cells stimulates GSK3-mediated LRP6 phosphorylation to promote Wnt signaling.
source: HGF-MET signaling in renal cells stimulates GSK3-mediated LRP6 phosphorylation to promote Wnt signaling (Monga et al., 2002; Koraishy et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: HGF-AKT signaling decreases GSK3 activity and increases β-catenin levels.
source: HGF-AKT signaling was shown to decrease GSK3 activity and increase β-catenin levels (Papkoff and Aikawa, 1998; Ishibe et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: MET can associate with and phosphorylate β-catenin, promoting its nuclear translocation and Wnt signaling.
source: MET can also associate with- and phosphorylate β-catenin, promoting its nuclear translocation and Wnt signaling (Monga et al., 2002; Apte et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: HGF signaling up-regulates Wnt ligands, integrins, and LEF1 to control downstream Wnt target gene activation.
source: Furthermore, HGF signaling up-regulates Wnt ligands, integrins, and LEF1 to control downstream Wnt target gene activation (Huang et al., 2012; Chaudhary et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In H1703 cells, downstream-acting mechanisms that bypass Wnts may not be involved in HGF-enhanced Wnt signaling.
source: However, in H1703 cells such downstream-acting mechanisms that bypass Wnts may not be involved since without Wnt3a, HGF did not induce β-catenin accumulation and because HGF-enhanced Wnt signaling was abolished by siZNRF3/RNF43 treatment (Figure 5D–E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the requirement for Wnt3a and ZNRF3/RNF43 for HGF effects in H1703 cells.

claim: ZNRF3 is a general inhibitor of Wnt receptors of both the LRP6 and FZD family.
source: ZNRF3 is a general inhibitor of Wnt receptors of both the LRP6 and FZD family (Hao et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: MET inhibiting ZNRF3 may upregulate canonical Wnt signaling and cross-talk with other FZD-dependent pathways such as Wnt/STOP, Wnt/PCP, and Wnt/Ca2+.
source: This suggests that MET inhibiting ZNRF3 may not only upregulate canonical Wnt signaling but also cross-talk with other FZD-dependent pathways such as Wnt/STOP (Taelman et al., 2010; Acebron et al., 2014), Wnt/PCP, and Wnt/Ca2+ (Miller et al., 1999; Hao et al., 2012; Tsukiyama et al., 2015), as well as BMPR1A-BMP4 signaling.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the known functions of ZNRF3, supported by citations.

claim: MET inhibiting ZNRF3 may cross-talk with BMPR1A-BMP4 signaling.
source: This suggests that MET inhibiting ZNRF3 may not only upregulate canonical Wnt signaling but also cross-talk with other FZD-dependent pathways such as Wnt/STOP (Taelman et al., 2010; Acebron et al., 2014), Wnt/PCP, and Wnt/Ca2+ (Miller et al., 1999; Hao et al., 2012; Tsukiyama et al., 2015), as well as BMPR1A-BMP4 signaling.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the known functions of ZNRF3.

claim: HGF-induced hyperactivation of BMP-SMAD signaling is consistent with MET cross-talk with BMP signaling via ZNRF3.
source: The reported HGF-induced hyperactivation of BMP-SMAD signaling would be consistent with this possibility (Addante et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an inference connecting reported observations to the current findings, supported by citation.

claim: MET and Wnt signaling share the property to stimulate cell proliferation, anti-apoptosis, angiogenesis, and invasive behavior.
source: The cross-talk between MET and Wnt signaling is cell-biologically intriguing because of their shared property to stimulate cell proliferation, anti-apoptosis, angiogenesis, and invasive behavior (Breuhahn et al., 2006; Gonzalez and Medici, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Both MET and Wnt pathways induce snail, a master regulator of invasion.
source: For example, both pathways induce a master regulator of invasion, snail (Saint-Jeannet et al., 1997; Grotegut et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: MET- and Wnt pathway activation are both prominently involved in colorectal cancer (CRC) progression.
source: MET- and Wnt pathway activation are also both prominently involved in colorectal cancer (CRC) progression (Bradley et al., 2017; Schatoff et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The majority of Wnt-pathway-dependent tumors are caused by mutations in APC that lead to ligand-receptor independent signaling.
source: While the majority of Wnt-pathway-dependent tumors are caused by mutations in APC (adenomatous polyposis coli) that lead to ligand-receptor independent signaling, there is a class of tumors that requires Wnt-receptor signaling and displays distinct molecular pathogenesis, morphology, and prognosis (Kleeman and Leedham, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: There is a class of tumors that requires Wnt-receptor signaling and displays distinct molecular pathogenesis, morphology, and prognosis.
source: While the majority of Wnt-pathway-dependent tumors are caused by mutations in APC (adenomatous polyposis coli) that lead to ligand-receptor independent signaling, there is a class of tumors that requires Wnt-receptor signaling and displays distinct molecular pathogenesis, morphology, and prognosis (Kleeman and Leedham, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Therapy of Wnt-receptor-dependent tumors may benefit from combined MET and Wnt inhibitor treatment by promoting ZNRF3 trafficking and Wnt receptor clearance.
source: Our results suggest that therapy of this subclass of tumors may benefit from combined MET and Wnt inhibitor treatment by promoting ZNRF3 trafficking and Wnt receptor clearance.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential therapeutic applications based on the findings.
